course.title: Learning How to Learn
course.description: A practical, evidence-based tour of how learning actually works — memory, spacing, self-testing, interleaving, and focus — so you can study less and remember more. Built from openly-licensed OER Commons — Study Skills & Learning material (CC BY) and grounded in cognitive-science research on the spacing effect, the testing effect, and interleaving.

questions.prompt: Which study method leads to the strongest long-term memory?
questions.explanation: Retrieving information from memory (self-testing) beats re-reading — this is the 'testing effect', covered in 'Active recall'.

questions.prompt: The 'forgetting curve' describes how memory…
options: decays quickly unless the material is revisited
questions.explanation: Newly learned material fades fast; spaced review flattens the curve — see 'Spaced practice'.

questions.prompt: Spacing your study across several days rather than one long session mainly helps because…
options: it feels easier at the time
each recall after forgetting a little strengthens memory
it avoids the need to review
questions.explanation: The 'desirable difficulty' of recalling partly-forgotten material builds durable memory — see 'Spaced practice'.

questions.prompt: Mixing several problem types in one session (rather than blocking one type) is called…
questions.explanation: Interleaving trains you to choose the right approach — see 'Interleaving & elaboration'.

questions.prompt: The idea that you learn best when taught in 'your learning style' (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) is…
options: a popular myth not supported by evidence
questions.explanation: Controlled studies find no benefit from matching teaching to a supposed style — see 'Active recall'.

questions.prompt: 'Elaboration' as a study strategy means…
options: explaining ideas in your own words and linking them to what you know
questions.explanation: Connecting new material to prior knowledge deepens encoding — see 'Interleaving & elaboration'.

questions.prompt: The Pomodoro method fights procrastination mainly by…
options: shrinking the task into a short, defined block of focused work
questions.explanation: A small, timed commitment lowers the activation cost of starting — see 'Focus & the Pomodoro method'.

questions.prompt: Metacognition means…
options: thinking about and steering your own learning
questions.explanation: Planning, monitoring, and reflecting on how you learn is metacognition — a thread through the whole course.

lessons.title: How memory and learning work
lessons.grammar_note: Three steps to remember: encode → store → retrieve. Learning is what survives retrieval.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the three stages of memory and explain why 'feeling familiar' with material is not the same as being able to recall it. Warm-up: think of a time you recognized an answer once you saw it but couldn't produce it on your own — which stage failed?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every memory passes through three stages: *encoding* (getting information in), *storage* (holding it over time), and *retrieval* (pulling it back out when you need it). Here is the trap almost every learner falls into: re-reading and highlighting make material feel *fluent* and familiar, and we mistake that fluency for learning. But an exam, a conversation, or a real task never asks you to recognize — it asks you to *retrieve*. Learning is best measured by what you can pull back out later, not by how smooth the page felt while you read it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Passive study: you read a page on the water cycle three times. It feels obvious, so you move on. Active study: after one read you close the book and write, from memory, the steps evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection, then check. The second approach feels harder and slower — and that difficulty is exactly why it builds a memory you can retrieve next week. Turning 're-read it' into 'recall it, then check' is the single highest-leverage change in this course.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each situation, name the failing stage (encoding, storage, or retrieval): (1) you were scrolling your phone during the lecture and none of it stuck; (2) a name is 'on the tip of your tongue'; (3) you learned a formula last month and now can't reconstruct it at all; (4) you understood the idea while reading but drew a blank in the quiz. Answers: (1) encoding, (2) retrieval, (3) storage/retrieval decay, (4) retrieval (recognition felt like learning).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating fluency ('this looks familiar') as proof you've learned it. Mistake: thinking memory is a video recording — it is reconstructive and can be reshaped each time you recall. Exit ticket: (a) Name the three memory stages in order. (b) Why is recognizing an answer weaker evidence of learning than producing it? Answers: encode, store, retrieve; because tests and real tasks require retrieval, and recognition can succeed even when retrieval would fail.

lessons.title: Spaced practice and the forgetting curve
lessons.grammar_note: Space it out: short reviews on days 1, 3, 7, and 14 beat one long cram.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the forgetting curve and design a spaced review schedule for a topic. Warm-up: after a single study session, roughly how much do you think you'd forget by tomorrow if you never looked at it again — 10%, or closer to half?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Newly learned material decays fast: the *forgetting curve*, first charted by Hermann Ebbinghaus, shows memory dropping steeply within hours and days unless it is revisited. The fix is *spaced practice* — spreading study across multiple sessions with gaps between them, instead of massing it all at once (cramming). Each time you return after forgetting a little and successfully recall the material, you push the curve higher and flatter. Decades of experiments show spaced study produces far better long-term retention than the same total time crammed together, even though cramming feels more productive in the moment.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Two students each spend two hours learning 40 vocabulary terms. Student A crams both hours the night before the test and scores well the next morning — then forgets most of it within a week. Student B splits the two hours into four 30-minute sessions on days 1, 3, 7, and 14, quizzing from memory each time. Student A wins tomorrow; Student B wins the month, the final, and the year. Note the mechanism: B lets a little forgetting happen on purpose, because recalling something you *almost* lost is what strengthens it — a 'desirable difficulty'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: You have a test in 12 days and about 90 minutes of total study to give a chapter. (1) Sketch a spaced schedule (which days, roughly how long each). (2) What should each session consist of — re-reading or self-quizzing? (3) Why not just do all 90 minutes tonight? (4) Name the phenomenon that makes tonight's cram fade. Sample answers: (1) ~20 min on days 1, 4, 8, 11; (2) mostly self-quizzing from memory, then checking; (3) massed practice fades fast and skips the strengthening effect of spaced recall; (4) the forgetting curve.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: judging a method by how good it feels now — cramming feels efficient precisely because the material is still fresh, which is the illusion. Mistake: spacing the sessions but only re-reading in each one; the gaps help most when each session is active recall. Exit ticket: (a) What does spacing do to the forgetting curve? (b) Why is a bit of forgetting between sessions useful? Answers: it raises and flattens it, slowing decay; recalling partly-forgotten material is harder and that effort builds a stronger, more durable memory.

lessons.title: Active recall and self-testing
lessons.grammar_note: Close the book and ask 'what do I remember?' — testing is studying, not just checking.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use active recall (self-testing) as your primary study tool and explain why it beats re-reading. Warm-up: when you 'review', do you usually look *at* the material or try to produce it *without* looking? Which one is your default?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The *testing effect* (also called retrieval practice) is one of the most robust findings in learning science: the act of retrieving information from memory strengthens that memory more than restudying it. A test is not just a measurement — it is one of the best *learning events* available. In a classic study, learners who studied a passage once and then repeatedly tested themselves remembered far more a week later than learners who studied the passage four times. A quick word on a persistent myth: the popular idea that you must be taught in your personal 'learning style' (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) has been tested directly and fails — matching instruction to a supposed style does not improve learning. What actually helps is choosing the format the *material* demands and retrieving it actively.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Passive re-reading, converted to active recall: instead of reading your biology notes for the fourth time, you cover them and answer aloud, 'What are the stages of mitosis, and what happens in each?' Then you uncover and check. Practical tools that force retrieval: flashcards (question side up, answer from memory), blank-page 'brain dumps' where you write everything you remember on a topic before checking, and past-paper questions done closed-book. Each one replaces looking-at with producing-from-memory.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Turn each passive habit into an active-recall version: (1) 'I re-read the chapter summary.' (2) 'I highlight key sentences.' (3) 'I copy the lecture slides.' (4) 'I look over the worked examples.' Sample answers: (1) close the book and write the summary from memory, then compare; (2) turn each key sentence into a question and answer it closed-book; (3) watch/read once, then reconstruct the slide's point from memory; (4) cover the solution and attempt the problem yourself before checking.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: peeking. If you glance back before genuinely trying to retrieve, you get re-reading, not testing. Mistake: believing the learning-styles myth and waiting for the 'right' format instead of just practicing recall. Mistake: only testing at the very end 'to see if you're ready' — test *throughout* to build the memory. Exit ticket: (a) Why does self-testing outperform re-reading? (b) True or false: teaching to a student's learning style reliably improves results. Answers: retrieval effort strengthens memory (the testing effect), while re-reading only boosts familiarity; false — the learning-styles claim is not supported by evidence.

questions.prompt: 'Learning is best measured by what you can retrieve later, not by how fluent the page felt.' This warns against trusting…
options: the feeling of familiarity from re-reading
questions.explanation: Fluency is an illusion of competence; retrieval is the real test.

questions.prompt: Compared with cramming two hours the night before, spacing the same two hours over two weeks usually produces…
questions.explanation: Spaced practice greatly improves durable retention.

questions.prompt: The testing effect says that retrieving information…
options: should be saved for exam day
questions.explanation: Retrieval practice is a learning event, not just measurement.

questions.prompt: A 'brain dump' — writing everything you remember on a blank page before checking — is an example of…
questions.explanation: It forces retrieval from memory.

questions.prompt: The claim that matching teaching to a student's 'learning style' improves learning is…
options: a myth not supported by evidence
questions.explanation: Direct tests find no benefit from style-matching.

questions.prompt: Letting a little forgetting happen between study sessions is useful because…
options: recalling partly-forgotten material builds stronger memory
it removes the need to review
questions.explanation: This 'desirable difficulty' strengthens retention.

lessons.title: Interleaving and elaboration
lessons.grammar_note: Mix problem types (interleave) and explain in your own words (elaborate).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Interleave related topics in a study session and use elaboration to deepen understanding. Warm-up: when you practice math or vocabulary, do you finish all of one type before moving on, or mix them? Which do you think feels harder?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Interleaving* means mixing different but related problem types or topics within a single session, instead of *blocking* (all of type A, then all of type B). Blocking feels smoother and boosts confidence, but interleaving forces you to notice differences and *choose* the right method each time — the exact skill a test or real problem demands. Studies of math and category learning repeatedly show interleaved practice produces better later performance, even when it felt worse during study. *Elaboration* is the partner strategy: explaining ideas in your own words, asking 'why' and 'how', and connecting new material to what you already know. The richer the connections, the more retrieval routes you build to reach a memory later.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Blocked practice: ten problems on area of a circle, then ten on volume of a sphere. You breeze through each block because you already know which formula to use. Interleaved practice: the twenty problems are shuffled, so before each one you must decide *which* formula applies — the same judgment the exam requires. For elaboration: instead of memorizing 'the spacing effect improves retention', you say, 'It works because each spaced recall makes me retrieve a partly-forgotten memory, and that effort strengthens it — like the desirable-difficulty idea from the last lesson.' You've just linked three concepts together.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) You're revising French verb tenses (present, past, future). Describe a blocked schedule and an interleaved one. (2) Why does the interleaved version transfer better to a real conversation? (3) Elaborate on 'active recall beats re-reading' by giving the reason in your own words. (4) Name one topic from your own studies where mixing types would help. Sample answers: (1) blocked = all present, then all past, then all future; interleaved = shuffled sentences requiring you to pick the tense each time; (2) real speech never announces the tense, so practicing the choice matters; (3) recall forces effortful retrieval that strengthens memory, re-reading only boosts familiarity; (4) any answer where distinct problem types are easily confused.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: abandoning interleaving because it feels harder and slower — that difficulty is the point and predicts better retention. Mistake: 'elaborating' by just copying longer notes; real elaboration is explaining *why* and linking ideas, not adding words. Exit ticket: (a) What judgment does interleaving force that blocking hides? (b) In one sentence, what does elaboration add to plain memorization? Answers: choosing the correct method/approach for each problem; it builds meaningful connections to prior knowledge, creating more routes to retrieve the memory.

lessons.title: Focus, procrastination, and the Pomodoro method
lessons.grammar_note: Start small: one 25-minute focused block beats waiting to 'feel ready'. Plan, monitor, reflect.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Run a focused study block using the Pomodoro method and use metacognition to steer your studying. Warm-up: what usually pulls your attention away mid-study — and how long after sitting down does it take you to actually start?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Procrastination is rarely laziness; it's usually the *activation cost* of starting a task that feels large or unpleasant, made worse by constant switching. The *Pomodoro method* attacks both: you commit to one small, defined block — classically 25 minutes of single-tasking — then take a 5-minute break, repeating in cycles. Shrinking the commitment lowers the cost of starting, and the timer protects one block from the endless pull of notifications. Focus is also fragile: every time you check your phone, the *switch cost* of getting back into deep work can run several minutes, so 'multitasking' silently taxes you. Wrapping all of this is *metacognition* — planning what and how you'll study, monitoring whether it's working mid-session, and reflecting afterward to adjust. The best students aren't just working hard; they're watching and steering how they work.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Turning a stalled session into a working one: instead of 'study biology' (vague, huge, easy to avoid), you set a Pomodoro: 'For 25 minutes, closed-book, I will recall and write the stages of cellular respiration, phone in another room.' At the beep you take 5 minutes off, then reflect: 'Retrieval on glycolysis was shaky — next block starts there.' That reflection is metacognition in action: you noticed a weak spot and re-planned. Notice how the block also uses active recall and produces its own spaced-review target for tomorrow — the strategies stack.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Rewrite the vague goal 'do some math revision' as a single concrete Pomodoro block. (2) Name two things you'd remove from your desk/phone to protect the block. (3) After the block, what one metacognitive question should you ask? (4) Why does checking your phone 'just for a second' cost more than a second? Sample answers: (1) e.g. '25 min, closed-book, 8 mixed problems on derivatives, checking answers at the end'; (2) e.g. phone in another room, notifications off, unrelated tabs closed; (3) 'What did I struggle to recall, and what should the next block target?'; (4) switch cost — it takes several minutes to rebuild focus after an interruption.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: waiting to 'feel motivated' before starting — action usually comes before motivation, so start a tiny block first. Mistake: treating breaks as optional and grinding until you fade; short breaks sustain focus across the session. Mistake: never reflecting, so you repeat the same ineffective session. Exit ticket: (a) How does a Pomodoro block lower the cost of starting? (b) Name the three metacognitive moves that steer good studying. Answers: it shrinks the task to one small, time-boxed, single-focus commitment; plan, monitor, and reflect.

options: forces you to choose the right method each time
questions.explanation: Interleaving practices the judgment real tasks require.

options: explaining why a concept works in your own words
questions.explanation: Elaboration means explaining and connecting, not adding words.

re-read once more to be sure

lessons.title: Applied project: design your own evidence-based study plan

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one real goal you actually care about — an upcoming exam, a language you're learning, a certification, or a skill like coding or an instrument. You will design a concrete, evidence-based study plan for it that puts this course's strategies to work. You won't just describe the strategies; you'll commit them to a real schedule you could start this week.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the goal, your deadline, and how you'll know you've succeeded (the measurable outcome). 2) Build a spaced schedule across the available days — list the sessions and roughly how long each. 3) For a typical session, specify the active-recall tools you'll use (flashcards, brain dumps, closed-book problems) instead of re-reading. 4) Show where you'll interleave topics rather than block them. 5) Add one elaboration habit (e.g. 'explain each new idea aloud as if teaching it'). 6) Define your focus protocol: Pomodoro block length, what you'll remove to protect it, and where breaks go. 7) Write one metacognitive checkpoint — a question you'll ask after each session to decide what the next one targets.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The goal is specific with a measurable success signal, not just 'get better'. ✔ Study is spaced across multiple days, not massed into one block. ✔ The plan's core activity is retrieval practice, not re-reading or highlighting. ✔ At least one place deliberately interleaves topics. ✔ An elaboration habit is named. ✔ A concrete focus protocol (Pomodoro + distraction removal) is defined. ✔ A reflection/monitoring step lets you adjust the plan. If all seven are true, you've built a plan grounded in how learning actually works — and you're now steering your own learning instead of guessing.
